claims.text: A machine-learning potential can predict free energies for both solid and fluid states near phase transitions.
The proposed potential can retain vibrational-entropy contributions.
The proposed potential can retain anharmonic contributions.
The proposed potential can retain electron–vibration coupling.
The proposed potential will substantially reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD.
An ab initio training dataset spanning high-entropy systems can support development of the proposed potential.
The proposed method is applicable from 500 K to 2000 K.
The machine-learning potential will learn relationships between atomic structure and free energy.
Learning structure–free-energy relationships will permit accurate prediction of thermodynamic properties.
Computational cost will be reduced by at least 50% relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
Computational cost will be reduced by at least 50% relative to TOR-TILD.
Phase free energies will be predicted with at least 90% accuracy.
Derived observables will be predicted with at least 90% accuracy.
The proposed method is applicable to systems containing up to five components.
Prediction accuracy may be limited by training-data quality.
Prediction accuracy may be limited by training-data quantity.
Prediction accuracy may be limited by the complexity of high-entropy systems.
The benchmark will compare the machine-learning potential with explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
The benchmark will measure phase free energies, entropy, and heat capacity.
The hypothesis is falsified if predictions fail to reach 90% accuracy for at least 80% of benchmark systems.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome broadly requires at least 90% accuracy, but the falsification rule only rejects the hypothesis when that accuracy is missed for at least 80% of systems. Thus, success on only slightly more than 20% of systems could avoid falsification despite not supporting the stated general performance claim.
Reduced computational cost is a central claim, including a quantified 50% reduction, but the falsification rule tests only predictive accuracy and cannot falsify the cost claim.
